Jira Extension Field Guide

A Chrome extension that adds Jira ticket shortcuts and SAP time logging to the toolbar — so mail replies, ticket transitions, and time entries happen without leaving the ticket. This guide walks through every tab and every screen, with screenshots from a live session.

00 — Overview

One toolbar icon, four jobs

The extension only activates its ticket actions on issue.swisscom.ch issue pages. Clicking the icon opens a popup with four tabs: the current ticket's actions, a personal issues board, a SAP session keep‑alive, and a queue of time entries waiting to be reconciled.

02

This JIRA — mail & ticket actions

The default tab. Everything here is gated on the active browser tab actually being a Jira issue page — off it, the icon row disables and a warning banner replaces the ticket actions.

The template list doubles as the mail composer: each entry is a saved body text configured in Options, and No template sends with just the ticket URL. The icon row below handles the four one‑click ticket actions, and the green bar opens the time‑logging form.
Why the warning banner appears Mail, Assign, Resolve, Label, and Copy ID all read the ticket key from the active tab's URL. Open the popup anywhere else and popup.js disables the icon row up front instead of letting each action fail after the click.
03

Log Time

Posts directly to SAP's ZONETIME5 Fiori app via its OData service, using a Time entry profile configured once in Options.

Opening the form pre‑fills the start time from where your last entry today left off (adding a forced lunch hour if it lands 12:00–13:00), suggests a profile matched to the current ticket's Jira project prefix, and reads the ITSM reference straight from the issue — the prefix bar at the top previews exactly what gets prepended to the SAP comment.
  1. Duration chips (15m…2h) set the End time from Start with one click; editing either field manually clears the active chip.
  2. The Profile dropdown sorts profiles matching the ticket's Jira project first, then by Incident/RFC type.
  3. Comment chips insert a preset investigation text, which you can still edit before submitting.
  4. The ↻ button fetches a fresh SAP Session ID — Chrome's own cookie jar first, the Edge bridge as fallback.
Redacted in these two screenshots The ITSM prefix bar (real incident number) and the Session ID value (a live SAP auth token) are blacked out — everything else in the form is exactly what you'll see.
04

Issues board

Runs three configured Jira Quick Filters against a Rapid View board and buckets the results into four worklist sections — a personal triage view without opening the full board.

Rows carry a left border stripe when a due date is close (amber) or already past (red, with a warning glyph). Unassigned rows get an inline assign button; the toolbar can group everything by project and flip sort direction. A background alarm refreshes the cache every few minutes, so most popup opens read from cache rather than hitting Jira live.
Redacted in this screenshot Ticket keys and summaries are blacked out (real incident content); project codes, statuses, and due dates are left visible — that's what drives the overdue/due‑soon highlighting shown here.
05

OneTime — session keep‑alive

Loads the real SAP OneTime Fiori app in a hidden iframe, scaled down to fit the popup, and reloads it every two minutes for as long as the popup stays open.

This is a genuine page navigation rather than a background fetch, so SAP's Set-Cookie response actually refreshes the session cookie in Chrome's cookie jar — something a fetch‑based keep‑alive ping can't do. It rides whatever SAP session is already active in Chrome; log in once in a normal tab and every popup open afterward extends it.
06

TO_BE_MODIFIED

A TO_BE_MODIFIED entry is a SAP time entry posted with a placeholder comment — used when the PSP element and Issue reference aren't known yet at logging time. This tab lists them and resolves each one against a real profile.

The list is read from a local cache (only the refresh button triggers a live SAP fetch), so reopening the popup doesn't refetch every time. Both spellings — TO_BE_MODIFIED and TO BE MODIFIED — are treated as equivalent, since both occur in practice.
  1. Pick an entry from the list and click Resolve.
  2. Enter the Issue reference (optional — there's no live Jira tab to auto‑detect it from here), choose a Time entry profile, and write the comment.
  3. Click Resolve… to see a confirmation summary before anything is sent.
  4. Confirm to apply — this overwrites the entry's type de prestation, PSP element, and position wholesale, not just the PSP, since placeholder entries have placeholder values across the board.
07

Options page

Everything the popup reads from is configured here once: templates, SAP identity, time profiles, and the Issues board's filter IDs.

Nine sections, top to bottom: Mail Provider, Mail Templates, INC Resolution Templates, Label Templates, Copy ID Comments, Employee Number, Default Start Time, Time Entry Profiles, Time Comment Templates, and the Jira Issues Board filter IDs. Every template list follows the same Edit/Delete pattern with an inline form.
Time entry profile — what "applying" one overwrites A profile bundles name, type de prestation, PSP element, and position. Applying one to a TO_BE_MODIFIED entry replaces all four on that entry, not just the PSP element — every field on a placeholder entry is placeholder, so a partial overwrite would leave it half‑fixed.
08

SAP session bridge

SAP's time tracker authenticates via Kerberos. Edge handles that automatically on the corporate network; Chrome usually can't — so the session cookie has to be relayed in from wherever it does get issued.

Clicking ↻ next to Session ID tries Chrome's own cookie jar first. If Chrome already has a valid SAP_SESSIONID_P3L_100 cookie — because SSO also worked there, or you're logged into SAP directly in Chrome — that's used immediately and the bridge is never involved.
01 · Chrome Cookie jar (primary) chrome.cookies.get() reads the SAP session cookie directly, even if it's httpOnly.
not found
02 · Edge Kerberos auth Opening a SAP page in Edge authenticates automatically and sets the session cookie there.
→
03 · Bookmarklet Reads & relays A bookmarklet in Edge's bar reads the cookie and POSTs it to the local bridge.
→
04 · Bridge 127.0.0.1:27182 A small Node server holds the value in memory until the extension's ↻ fetches it.
Why a network relay instead of a shared cookie Chrome and Edge keep separate cookie jars even on the same machine, and the session cookie expires roughly every 10 minutes — so the bridge exists purely to move a short‑lived value from the browser that can authenticate to the one that can't, on demand.
Set the bridge to start automatically at login (Task Scheduler on Windows, a launchd agent on macOS — see bridge/install-autostart.*), and once it's running, drag the "↻ Send SAP Cookie" button from http://127.0.0.1:27182 into Edge's bookmarks bar.
